topic: Secure SDLC, threat modelling and testing

notes.front: What is threat modelling in secure software development?
notes.back: A form of risk modelling used during design to help assess the security risk of the software.
notes.explanation: The Secure Software Development Framework lists it alongside attack modelling and attack surface mapping.
notes.example: Like an architect walking round the plans of a bank asking where a burglar would try to get in, before any wall is built.
notes.evidence: Use forms of risk modeling – such as threat modeling, attack modeling, or attack surface mapping – to help assess the security risk for the software.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.1, Design Software to Meet Security Requirements and Mitigate Security Risks, PDF p. 20

notes.front: What is the STRIDE model?
notes.back: A model that sorts threats into six categories: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege.
notes.explanation: Microsoft uses it to help teams frame pointed questions about threats and to simplify security conversations.
notes.example: Like a checklist of six ways a house could be burgled, which you read out while looking at each door and window.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In STRIDE, what is spoofing?
notes.back: Pretending to be another user by using their sign-in details, such as a username and password, after getting hold of them illegally.
notes.explanation: It is the first of the six STRIDE threat categories.
notes.example: Like someone using a colleague’s swipe card to get into the office as if they were that colleague.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In STRIDE, what is tampering?
notes.back: The malicious modification of data, whether stored (for example in a database) or flowing between computers over an open network.
notes.explanation: Microsoft gives both data at rest and data in transit as targets.
notes.example: Like changing the amount on a cheque after it has been signed.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In STRIDE, what is repudiation?
notes.back: A user denies having done something, and nobody else can prove that they did.
notes.explanation: Microsoft’s example is an illegal operation in a system that cannot trace prohibited operations.
notes.example: Like a customer claiming a parcel never arrived when the courier took no signature or photograph.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD)?
notes.back: Automation in which tools test an app’s components and assemble them into a build, and tools then deploy each tested version to its target environment.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-190 describes both halves for container images: build tools test components and assemble images, and delivery tools deploy them.
notes.example: Like a bakery conveyor that mixes, bakes, checks and boxes each batch automatically, rather than a baker carrying trays between stations.
notes.evidence: Image creation typically uses build management and automation tools, such as Jenkins [8] and TeamCity [9], to assist with what is called the “continuous integration” process. These tools take the various libraries, binaries, and other components of an app, perform testing on them
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, Section 2.3.1 Image Creation, Testing, and Accreditation, PDF p. 21

notes.front: What is static application security testing (SAST)?
notes.back: Analysing code without running it, using tools that check for vulnerabilities and compliance with secure coding standards.
notes.explanation: The Secure Software Development Framework pairs the tool with a human who reviews and remediates what it reports.
notes.example: Like a proofreader checking a contract’s wording for loopholes before anyone signs it.
notes.evidence: Use a static analysis tool to automatically check code for vulnerabilities and compliance with the organization’s secure coding standards with a human reviewing the issues reported by the tool and remediating them as necessary.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.7, Review and/or Analyze Human-Readable Code, PDF p. 23

notes.front: What is dynamic application security testing (DAST)?
notes.back: Testing software while it runs, using tools that monitor it for problems such as memory corruption and user privilege issues.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-53 calls this dynamic code analysis: runtime verification that security functions work as designed.
notes.example: Like test-driving a car on a track and trying the brakes hard, rather than reading its blueprints.
notes.evidence: Dynamic code analysis provides runtime verification of software programs using tools capable of monitoring programs for memory corruption, user privilege issues, and other potential security problems.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(8) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Dynamic Code Analysis, PDF p. 306

notes.front: What is interactive application security testing (IAST)?
notes.back: Detecting vulnerabilities by observing an application as it runs during testing, using instrumentation.
notes.explanation: It is also known as instrumentation-based testing and draws on access to code, user interaction, libraries, frameworks and configurations.
notes.example: Like fitting sensors inside an engine during a test drive, so you see both the road behaviour and what each part is doing.
notes.evidence: Interactive (also known as instrumentation-based) application security testing is a method of detecting vulnerabilities by observing applications as they run during testing.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(9) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Interactive Application Security Testing, PDF p. 306

notes.front: What is software composition analysis (SCA)?
notes.back: Analysing the components that make up software, in source or binary form, to learn their provenance and assess the risk each may introduce.
notes.explanation: The Secure Software Development Framework lists it with a software bill of materials as a way to get provenance information for each component.
notes.example: Like reading the ingredients label on every jar you use in a recipe, to spot any recalled product.
notes.evidence: Obtain provenance information (e.g., SBOM, source composition analysis, binary software composition analysis) for each software component, and analyze that information to better assess the risk that the component may introduce.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.4, Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software, PDF p. 21

notes.front: What is broken access control?
notes.back: A failure of the controls meant to stop users acting outside their intended permissions.
notes.explanation: The Top 10:2025 page says such failures typically lead to unauthorised disclosure, modification or destruction of data, or business functions performed beyond the user’s limits.
notes.example: Like a hotel key card that opens every room on the floor, not just the guest’s own.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A01:2025 Broken Access Control, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an injection vulnerability?
notes.back: A flaw that lets untrusted user input reach an interpreter, such as a database or command line, which then runs part of it as commands.
notes.explanation: The Top 10:2025 page says the concept is the same whichever interpreter is involved.
notes.example: Like a clerk who reads a customer’s form aloud to the safe’s voice lock, and the “name” field says “open the safe”.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A05:2025 Injection, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is broken object level authorisation (BOLA)?
notes.back: An interface flaw where a function that takes an object identifier from the user fails to check the user may access that object.
notes.explanation: It ranks first in the 2023 list of security risks for application programming interfaces, which says such endpoints create a wide attack surface.
notes.example: Like a cloakroom that hands over any coat to whoever reads out a ticket number, without checking the ticket.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks – 2023, OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks – 2023, Risk Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the CWE Top 25?
notes.back: The Common Weakness Enumeration’s list of the 25 most dangerous software weaknesses: the most common and impactful ones.
notes.explanation: The list says these weaknesses are often easy to find and exploit, and can let adversaries take over a system, steal data or stop applications working.
notes.example: Like a road-safety list of the 25 junctions with the most crashes, so councils know where to fix things first.
notes.evidence: Welcome to the 2025 Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE™) Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses list (CWE™ Top 25). This list demonstrates the currently most common and impactful software weaknesses.
notes.source: MITRE, 2025 CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses, CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses
notes.sourceLicence: B · CWE terms of use (MITRE royalty-free licence)

notes.front: What is the Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS)?
notes.back: A standard from the Open Web Application Security Project for verifying application security; the Secure Software Development Framework cites version 4.0.3.
notes.explanation: The framework lists it among the references for some of its practices.
notes.example: Like a building inspector’s checklist that a new house is checked against before sign-off.
notes.evidence: Open Web Application Security Project (2021) OWASP Application Security Verification Standard 4.0.3.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, References, PDF p. 30

notes.front: What are two software development life cycle models the Secure Software Development Framework names?
notes.back: Any two of: waterfall, spiral, agile, and agile combined with DevOps practices.
notes.explanation: The framework notes there are many models, and names these as examples.
notes.evidence: There are many models for SDLCs, including waterfall, spiral, agile, and – in particular – agile combined with software development and IT operations (DevOps) practices.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: Why do secure development practices usually have to be added to a software development life cycle model?
notes.back: Few life cycle models explicitly address software security in detail.
notes.explanation: So the practices need to be added to, and integrated into, each model.
notes.evidence: Few SDLC models explicitly address software security in detail, so secure software development practices usually need to be added to and integrated into each SDLC model.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: What three reasons does the Secure Software Development Framework give for integrating secure practices throughout the life cycle?
notes.back: Fewer vulnerabilities in released software; less impact from undetected ones being exploited; root causes addressed to prevent recurrence.
notes.explanation: The framework says this applies whichever life cycle model is used.
notes.evidence: to reduce the number of vulnerabilities in released software, to reduce the potential impact of the exploitation of undetected or unaddressed vulnerabilities, and to address the root causes of vulnerabilities to prevent recurrences.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: Besides bugs from coding flaws, what are two sources of vulnerabilities the Secure Software Development Framework names?
notes.back: Any two of: security configuration settings, incorrect trust assumptions, outdated risk analysis.
notes.explanation: The framework widens “vulnerability” beyond coding errors on purpose.
notes.evidence: Vulnerabilities include not just bugs caused by coding flaws, but also weaknesses caused by security configuration settings, incorrect trust assumptions, and outdated risk analysis.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: Does the Secure Software Development Framework prescribe how to implement its practices?
notes.back: No. It identifies the practices and focuses on their outcomes, not on how to implement them.
notes.explanation: This leaves organisations free to fit the practices to their own life cycle model.
notes.evidence: This document identifies secure software development practices but does not prescribe how to implement them. The focus is on the outcomes of the practices to be implemented
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: Which group of the Secure Software Development Framework makes sure people, processes and technology are ready for secure development at organisation level?
notes.back: Prepare the Organisation.
notes.explanation: The framework adds that many of this group’s practices also apply to individual development groups or projects.
notes.evidence: Prepare the Organization (PO): Organizations should ensure that their people, processes, and technology are prepared to perform secure software development at the organization level.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 2 The Secure Software Development Framework, PDF p. 13

notes.front: Which group of the Secure Software Development Framework protects all components of the software from tampering and unauthorised access?
notes.back: Protect the Software.
notes.explanation: It is the second of the framework’s four practice groups.
notes.evidence: Protect the Software (PS): Organizations should protect all components of their software from tampering and unauthorized access.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 2 The Secure Software Development Framework, PDF p. 13

notes.front: Which group of the Secure Software Development Framework aims for well-secured software with minimal security vulnerabilities in its releases?
notes.back: Produce Well-Secured Software.
notes.explanation: It is the third of the framework’s four practice groups, and holds the design, review and testing practices.
notes.evidence: Produce Well-Secured Software (PW): Organizations should produce well-secured software with minimal security vulnerabilities in its releases.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 2 The Secure Software Development Framework, PDF p. 13

notes.front: Which group of the Secure Software Development Framework deals with residual vulnerabilities in released software?
notes.back: Respond to Vulnerabilities.
notes.explanation: It covers responding to those vulnerabilities and preventing similar ones in future.
notes.evidence: Respond to Vulnerabilities (RV): Organizations should identify residual vulnerabilities in their software releases and respond appropriately to address those vulnerabilities and prevent similar ones from occurring in the future.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 2 The Secure Software Development Framework, PDF p. 13

notes.front: What does the framework’s practice for verifying software release integrity help software acquirers do?
notes.back: Make sure the software they acquire is legitimate and has not been tampered with.
notes.explanation: One example is posting cryptographic hashes for release files.
notes.evidence: Help software acquirers ensure that the software they acquire is legitimate and has not been tampered with. PS.2.1: Make software integrity verification information available to software acquirers. Example 1: Post cryptographic hashes for release
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PS.2, Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity, PDF p. 19

notes.front: Why does the Secure Software Development Framework say to archive and protect each software release?
notes.back: To help identify, analyse and eliminate vulnerabilities discovered in the software after release.
notes.explanation: Archived files include integrity verification information and other supporting data.
notes.evidence: Preserve software releases in order to help identify, analyze, and eliminate vulnerabilities discovered in the software after release.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PS.3, Archive and Protect Each Software Release, PDF p. 19

notes.front: Why does the Secure Software Development Framework say to analyse the root causes of vulnerabilities over time?
notes.back: To identify patterns, such as a particular secure coding practice not being followed consistently.
notes.explanation: This sits in the Respond to Vulnerabilities group, after analysing each vulnerability’s root cause.
notes.evidence: Analyze the root causes over time to identify patterns, such as a particular secure coding practice not being followed consistently.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice RV.3, Analyze Vulnerabilities to Identify Their Root Causes, PDF p. 27

notes.front: Why does the Secure Software Development Framework recommend supporting toolchains?
notes.back: Automation reduces human effort and improves the accuracy, reproducibility, usability and comprehensiveness of security practices.
notes.explanation: It also provides a way to document and demonstrate that the practices are used.
notes.evidence: Use automation to reduce human effort and improve the accuracy, reproducibility, usability, and comprehensiveness of security practices throughout the SDLC, as well as provide a way to document and demonstrate the use of these practices.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PO.3, Implement Supporting Toolchains, PDF p. 16

notes.front: What are two ways the Secure Software Development Framework suggests for deploying and maintaining toolchains securely?
notes.back: Any two of: code-based configuration (pipelines-as-code), reproducible builds, updating or replacing tools to fix their vulnerabilities.
notes.explanation: These are among its implementation examples for following recommended practices for tools and toolchains.
notes.evidence: Example 3: Use code-based configuration for toolchains (e.g., pipelines-as-code, toolchains-as-code). Example 4: Implement the technologies and processes needed for reproducible builds. Example 5: Update, upgrade, or replace tools as needed to address tool vulnerabilities
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PO.3, Implement Supporting Toolchains, PDF p. 16

notes.front: In the “continuous delivery” automation Special Publication 800-190 describes, what does the developer do and what do the tools do?
notes.back: The developer builds, tests and pushes a new image to the registry; automation tools deploy it to the target environment.
notes.explanation: The guidance says this lets fixed app code be tested and deployed much faster.
notes.evidence: This “continuous delivery” automation enables developers to simply build a new version of the image for their app, test the image, push it to the registry, and then rely on the automation tools to deploy it to the target envi
notes.source: NIST SP 800-190, Application Container Security Guide, Section 2.3.3 Container Deployment and Management, PDF p. 23

notes.front: Where does the Secure Software Development Framework suggest more rigorous risk assessments during design?
notes.back: In high-risk areas, such as protecting sensitive data and safeguarding identification, authentication and access control.
notes.explanation: It is one implementation example for the risk-modelling task.
notes.evidence: Perform more rigorous assessments for high-risk areas, such as protecting sensitive data and safeguarding identification, authentication, and access control
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.1, Design Software to Meet Security Requirements and Mitigate Security Risks, PDF p. 20

notes.front: After modelling threats, what should a team record about each risk, according to the Secure Software Development Framework?
notes.back: The response to it, including how mitigations will be achieved and the rationale for any approved exceptions.
notes.explanation: Mitigations are then added to the software’s security requirements.
notes.evidence: Record the response to each risk, including how mitigations are to be achieved and what the rationales are for any approved exceptions to the security requirements. Add any mitigations to the software’s security requirements.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.1, Design Software to Meet Security Requirements and Mitigate Security Risks, PDF p. 20

notes.front: Why does Microsoft say its Threat Modeling Tool helps architects identify security issues early?
notes.back: Problems found at the design stage are fairly cheap and simple to fix, so the overall cost of development falls sharply.
notes.explanation: The tool is part of Microsoft’s Security Development Lifecycle and is designed with non-security experts in mind.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, Introduction
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which STRIDE category covers information reaching people who should not be able to see it?
notes.back: Information disclosure.
notes.explanation: Microsoft’s examples include reading a file without being granted access, and intercepting data in transit.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which STRIDE category covers attacks that deny service to valid users, such as making a web server temporarily unusable?
notes.back: Denial of service.
notes.explanation: Microsoft says some protection against it is needed simply to improve availability and reliability.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which STRIDE category covers a user without privileges obtaining privileged access, enough to compromise or wreck the whole system?
notes.back: Elevation of privilege.
notes.explanation: Microsoft calls the case where an attacker becomes part of the trusted system itself a dangerous situation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the STRIDE guidance, what is non-repudiation?
notes.back: A system's ability to defeat repudiation threats, for example by holding proof that an action took place.
notes.explanation: Microsoft’s example is a buyer signing for a parcel, so the vendor holds evidence of delivery.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Under the developer configuration management control of Special Publication 800-53, which changes may be implemented?
notes.back: Only organisation-approved changes, with the integrity of changes to configuration items documented, managed and controlled.
notes.explanation: Approved changes and their potential security and privacy impacts must also be documented.
notes.evidence: Document, manage, and control the integrity of changes to [Assignment: organizationdefined configuration items under configuration management]; c. Implement only organization-approved changes to the system, component, or service;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-10 Developer Configuration Management, PDF p. 300

notes.front: Why does developer configuration management need strict configuration control throughout the life cycle?
notes.back: To maintain the integrity of changes: tracking authorised changes and preventing unauthorised ones.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-53 also protects master copies of material used to generate security-relevant parts of the system.
notes.evidence: Maintaining the integrity of changes to the system, system component, or system service requires strict configuration control throughout the system development life cycle to track authorized changes and preve
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-10 Developer Configuration Management, PDF p. 301

notes.front: Developer configuration management also requires the developer to track {{c1::security flaws and flaw resolution}} and report findings to defined personnel.
notes.explanation: It is the last element of the control, after documenting approved changes and their impacts.
notes.evidence: Track security flaws and flaw resolution within the system, component, or service and report findings to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel].
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-10 Developer Configuration Management, PDF p. 301

notes.front: When is static code analysis most effective, according to Special Publication 800-53?
notes.back: Early in development, when each code change can be scanned automatically for potential weaknesses.
notes.explanation: It can then give clear remediation guidance and identify defects for developers to fix.
notes.evidence: It is most effective when used early in the development process, when each code change can automatically be scanned for potential weaknesses. Static code analysis can provide clear remediation guidance and identify defects for developers to fix.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(1) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Static Code Analysis, PDF p. 304

notes.front: Besides weaknesses in the code itself, what does static code analysis check for?
notes.back: Included libraries or other code with known vulnerabilities, or that are out of date and unsupported.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-53 says it can also enforce secure coding practices.
notes.evidence: includes checking for weaknesses in the code as well as for the incorporation of libraries or other included code with known vulnerabilities or that are out-of-date and not supported.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(1) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Static Code Analysis, PDF p. 304

notes.front: How does fuzz testing, a type of dynamic analysis, find flaws?
notes.back: By deliberately feeding malformed or random data into a program to induce failures.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-53 says fuzzing strategies come from the application’s intended use and its functional and design specifications.
notes.evidence: A type of dynamic analysis, known as fuzz testing, induces program failures by deliberately introducing malformed or random data into software programs.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(8) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Dynamic Code Analysis, PDF p. 306

notes.front: What does the Secure Software Development Framework suggest doing with dynamic vulnerability testing and with tests for previously reported vulnerabilities?
notes.back: Integrate dynamic vulnerability testing into the automated test suite, and add tests for past vulnerabilities so errors are not reintroduced.
notes.explanation: Both are examples under testing executable code to find vulnerabilities.
notes.evidence: Example 2: Integrate dynamic vulnerability testing into the project’s automated test suite. Example 3: Incorporate tests for previously reported vulnerabilities into the project’s test suite to ensure that errors are not reintroduced.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.8, Test Executable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities, PDF p. 24

notes.front: What kind of testing of security features does the Secure Software Development Framework give as its first example for testing executable code?
notes.back: Robust functional testing of security features.
notes.explanation: It appears alongside dynamic vulnerability testing, fuzzing and penetration testing.
notes.evidence: Example 1: Perform robust functional testing of security features.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.8, Test Executable Code to Identify Vulnerabilities, PDF p. 24

notes.front: When can instrumentation-based testing be used in the life cycle?
notes.back: In real time and continuously throughout the system development life cycle.
notes.explanation: Combined with analysis techniques, it can find a broad range of vulnerabilities and confirm that controls work.
notes.evidence: identify a broad range of potential vulnerabilities and confirm control effectiveness. Instrumentation-based testing works in real time and can be used continuously throughout the system development life cycle.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(9) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Interactive Application Security Testing, PDF p. 306

notes.front: What can a toolchain do automatically to keep third-party components meeting requirements?
notes.back: Detect known vulnerabilities in software components.
notes.explanation: The Secure Software Development Framework also suggests regularly checking for publicly known vulnerabilities that vendors have not yet fixed.
notes.evidence: Example 1: Regularly check whether there are publicly known vulnerabilities in the software modules and services that vendors have not yet fixed. Example 2: Build into the toolchain automatic detection of known vulnerabilities in software components.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.4, Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software, PDF p. 22

notes.front: Which three styles of penetration testing does Special Publication 800-53 name?
notes.back: White-box, gray-box and black-box testing.
notes.explanation: All are analyses by skilled professionals who simulate adversary actions.
notes.evidence: Penetration testing can include white-box, gray-box, or black-box testing with analyses performed by skilled professionals who simulate adversary actions.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(5) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Penetration Testing, PDF p. 305

notes.front: What are two kinds of information Special Publication 800-53 says are useful to penetration testers?
notes.back: Any two of: product and system design specifications, source code, administrator and operator manuals.
notes.explanation: Assessors use all available documentation to try to circumvent the implemented security and privacy features.
notes.evidence: Useful information for assessors who conduct penetration testing includes product and system design specifications, source code, and administrator and operator manuals.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(5) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Penetration Testing, PDF p. 305

notes.front: What is the purpose of covert (black hat) security testing?
notes.back: To examine the damage or impact an adversary can cause, not to identify vulnerabilities.
notes.explanation: It is done without the knowledge of the organisation’s technology staff but with the permission of upper management.
notes.evidence: Covert testing may be conducted with or without warning. The purpose of covert testing is to examine the damage or impact an adversary can cause—it does not focus on identifying vulnerabilities.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment, Section 2.4.2 Overt and Covert, PDF p. 16

notes.front: What are two kinds of developer testing Special Publication 800-53 lets an organisation select under its developer testing and evaluation control?
notes.back: Any two of: unit, integration, system, regression testing.
notes.explanation: The developer must also produce evidence of the testing and correct the flaws it finds.
notes.evidence: Perform [Selection (one or more): unit; integration; system; regression] testing/evaluation
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11 Developer Testing and Evaluation, PDF p. 303

notes.front: What is the Open Web Application Security Project’s Top 10?
notes.back: A standard awareness document for developers on web application security: a broad consensus on the most critical security risks to web applications.
notes.explanation: The current edition, released in 2025, updates the list based on the latest data and security trends.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, Welcome to the OWASP Top 10:2025 Release
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which category ranks first in the Top 10:2025 list of web application security risks?
notes.back: Broken Access Control.
notes.explanation: It is number 1 of the ten categories in the 2025 edition, which updates the list from the latest data and trends.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, Top 10:2025 List
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which category ranks second in the Top 10:2025 list of web application security risks?
notes.back: Security Misconfiguration.
notes.explanation: It is number 2 of the ten categories in the 2025 edition, which updates the list from the latest data and trends.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, Top 10:2025 List
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which category ranks third in the Top 10:2025 list of web application security risks?
notes.back: Software Supply Chain Failures.
notes.explanation: It is number 3 of the ten categories in the 2025 edition, which updates the list from the latest data and trends.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, Top 10:2025 List
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which category ranks fourth in the Top 10:2025 list of web application security risks?
notes.back: Cryptographic Failures.
notes.explanation: It is number 4 of the ten categories in the 2025 edition, which updates the list from the latest data and trends.

notes.front: What are two common access control vulnerabilities the Top 10:2025 page describes?
notes.back: Any two of: no deny by default, bypassing checks by altering requests, viewing another account via its identifier, force browsing, among others.
notes.explanation: All let a user act outside intended permissions.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A01:2025 Broken Access Control, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where does the Top 10:2025 page say access control is effective, and what should the default be for non-public resources?
notes.back: Only in trusted server-side code or serverless interfaces the attacker cannot modify; deny by default.
notes.explanation: Controls in code the attacker can change can simply be altered.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A01:2025 Broken Access Control, How to prevent
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are two common kinds of injection the Top 10:2025 page names?
notes.back: Any two of: Structured Query Language, NoSQL, operating system command, object relational mapping, expression language injection, among others.
notes.explanation: The page says the concept is identical across all interpreters.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A05:2025 Injection, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Top 10:2025 page call the best means of preventing injection?
notes.back: Keeping data separate from commands and queries, preferably through a safe interface that avoids the interpreter or is parameterised.
notes.explanation: Server-side input validation helps but the page says it is not a complete defence.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A05:2025 Injection, How to prevent
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the Top 10:2025 page say injection is best detected?
notes.back: Source code review combined with automated testing, including fuzzing, of all inputs.
notes.explanation: It adds that static, dynamic and interactive testing tools in the delivery pipeline can help catch injection before production.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A05:2025 Injection, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What are software supply chain failures?
notes.back: Breakdowns or compromises in building, distributing or updating software, often from flawed or malicious third-party code, tools or dependencies.
notes.explanation: The Top 10:2025 page lists untracked component versions, including transitive dependencies, as one sign of exposure.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What separation of duty does the Top 10:2025 page expect in a software supply chain?
notes.back: No single person should be able to write code and promote it all the way to production without oversight.
notes.explanation: The page treats a supply chain without separation of duty as a sign of vulnerability.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What three failings can make up mishandling of exceptional conditions?
notes.back: Not preventing an unusual situation, not identifying it as it happens, and responding poorly or not at all afterwards.
notes.explanation: The page says any time an application is unsure of its next instruction, an exceptional condition has been mishandled.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A10:2025 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the European cyber-security agency’s 2009 assessment characterise the malicious insider risk in cloud computing?

notes.front: What is loss of governance in the European cyber-security agency’s 2009 cloud risk assessment?

notes.front: An attacker on a café’s open wi-fi alters the prices in an order as it travels to an online shop. Which STRIDE category is this?
notes.back: Tampering.
notes.choices:
A) Spoofing
B) Tampering
C) Repudiation
notes.choicesExplained: A: spoofing uses someone else’s authentication information; nothing is impersonated here. C: repudiation is denying an action with no way to prove otherwise.
notes.explanation: Malicious modification of data as it flows between two computers over an open network is tampering.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A customer insists she never placed a large order, and the shop’s system kept no record that could show who did. Which STRIDE category is the shop exposed to?
notes.back: Repudiation.
notes.choices:
A) Spoofing
B) Tampering
C) Repudiation
notes.choicesExplained: A: no one is shown to have used her credentials. B: no data was shown to be maliciously altered.
notes.explanation: A user denying an action when the system cannot prove otherwise is repudiation.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A criminal buys a leaked username and password and signs in to a payroll portal as the employee. Which STRIDE category is this?
notes.back: Spoofing.
notes.choices:
A) Spoofing
B) Tampering
C) Repudiation
notes.choicesExplained: B: signing in with stolen credentials alters no data by itself. C: repudiation is about denying an action, not impersonation.
notes.explanation: Using another user’s authentication information after obtaining it illegally is spoofing.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A support engineer finds he can open other teams’ salary spreadsheets on a shared drive that he was never granted access to. Which STRIDE category is this?
notes.back: Information disclosure.
notes.choices:
A) Information disclosure
B) Elevation of privilege
C) Denial of service
notes.choicesExplained: B: he reads files but gains no privileged access to compromise the system. C: no valid user is denied service.
notes.explanation: Exposure of information to people not supposed to have access, such as reading an ungranted file, is information disclosure.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: On a billing site, a customer changes the invoice number in the web address and sees another customer’s invoice. Which Top 10:2025 category is this?
notes.back: Broken Access Control.
notes.choices:
A) Injection
B) Broken Access Control
C) Cryptographic Failures
notes.choicesExplained: A: no input is run as a command by an interpreter. C: nothing here involves weak or missing cryptography.
notes.explanation: Viewing someone else’s account by supplying its identifier is one of the access control flaws the page lists.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A01:2025 Broken Access Control, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Text typed into a shop’s search box is pasted straight into a database query, and a crafted search returns every customer’s details. Which Top 10:2025 category is this?
notes.back: Injection.
notes.choices:
A) Injection
B) Security Misconfiguration
C) Broken Access Control
notes.choicesExplained: B: the flaw is in how input is handled, not in a configuration setting. C: the query itself was subverted; no access check was bypassed by changing an identifier.
notes.explanation: Untrusted input reaching an interpreter, which runs part of it as a command, is injection.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A05:2025 Injection, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A mobile banking interface returns account details for whatever account number the app sends, without checking it belongs to the signed-in user. Which 2023 interface security risk is this?
notes.back: Broken object level authorisation.

A) Broken object level authorisation
B) Broken Authentication
C) Unrestricted Resource Consumption
notes.choicesExplained: B: the user is properly signed in; the missing check is on the object. C: no resource is being exhausted.
notes.explanation: A function that takes an object identifier from the user without an object level authorisation check fits this risk.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks – 2023, OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks – 2023, Risk Description

notes.front: A team wants every code change checked for vulnerable patterns and out-of-date libraries automatically, before the code is ever run. Which testing approach fits?
notes.back: Static application security testing.
notes.choices:
A) Static application security testing
B) Dynamic application security testing
C) Covert security testing
notes.choicesExplained: B: dynamic testing needs the program running. C: covert testing examines the damage an adversary could cause to a live system.
notes.explanation: Static analysis checks the code and included libraries without running it, and works best when each change is scanned early.
notes.evidence: It is most effective when used early in the development process, when each code change can automatically be scanned for potential weaknesses.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(1) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Static Code Analysis, PDF p. 304

notes.front: Testers send thousands of random and malformed requests to a running web service to see whether it crashes. Which kind of testing is this?
notes.back: Fuzz testing, a form of dynamic analysis.
notes.choices:
A) Static code analysis
B) Fuzz testing
C) Software composition analysis
notes.choicesExplained: A: static analysis examines code without running it. C: composition analysis examines the components the software is made from.
notes.explanation: Deliberately feeding malformed or random data to induce failures is fuzz testing, which is dynamic.
notes.evidence: A type of dynamic analysis, known as fuzz testing, induces program failures by deliberately introducing malformed or random data into software programs.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(8) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Dynamic Code Analysis, PDF p. 306

notes.front: A company wants to know which open-source libraries its product contains, where they came from and whether any has a known vulnerability. Which testing approach fits?
notes.back: Software composition analysis.
notes.choices:
A) Software composition analysis
B) Interactive application security testing
C) A tabletop exercise
notes.choicesExplained: B: interactive testing observes the running application, not its inventory of components. C: a tabletop exercise rehearses a contingency plan by discussion.
notes.explanation: Composition analysis gives provenance information for each component so its risk can be assessed.
notes.evidence: Obtain provenance information (e.g., SBOM, source composition analysis, binary software composition analysis) for each software component
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.4, Reuse Existing, Well-Secured Software, PDF p. 21

notes.front: A software vendor publishes cryptographic hashes of each release so customers can check their downloads. Which group of the Secure Software Development Framework does this belong to?
notes.back: Protect the Software.
notes.choices:
A) Prepare the Organisation
B) Protect the Software
C) Respond to Vulnerabilities
notes.choicesExplained: A: that group readies people, processes and technology. C: that group handles residual vulnerabilities after release.
notes.explanation: Making integrity verification information available is a task under protecting the software.
notes.evidence: PS.2.1: Make software integrity verification information available to software acquirers. Example 1: Post cryptographic hashes for release
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PS.2, Provide a Mechanism for Verifying Software Release Integrity, PDF p. 19

notes.front: A team building a cloud service with agile and DevOps asks whether secure development practices apply only to waterfall projects. What does the Secure Software Development Framework say?
notes.back: They should be integrated throughout whichever life cycle model is used.
notes.choices:
A) They apply only to waterfall
B) They apply regardless of the model
C) Agile teams need no added practices
notes.choicesExplained: A: the framework ties them to no single model. C: few models address security in detail, so practices usually need adding.
notes.explanation: The framework applies regardless of model, and names agile with DevOps among the models.
notes.evidence: Regardless of which SDLC model is used, secure software development practices should be integrated throughout it
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Section 1 Introduction, PDF p. 10

notes.front: A cloud provider’s system administrator quietly copies a customer’s database to a personal drive. Which risk from the European cyber-security agency’s 2009 assessment is this?
notes.back: Malicious insider.
notes.choices:
A) Malicious insider
B) Isolation failure
C) Loss of governance
notes.choicesExplained: B: no tenant separation mechanism failed; the provider’s own staff misused access. C: loss of governance is ceding control through the contract, not a deliberate act.
notes.explanation: The agency singles out provider system administrators as an extremely high-risk role.
notes.source: ENISA, Cloud Computing: Benefits, risks and recommendations for information security (2009), Executive summary, Top security risks, PDF p. 10
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A developer pushes a quick fix straight to production outside the change process, and nobody records it. Which requirement of developer configuration management is broken?
notes.back: Implementing only organisation-approved changes, and documenting them.
notes.choices:
A) Implementing only approved, documented changes
B) Correlating audit records
C) Physical access control
notes.choicesExplained: B: correlating audit records is a monitoring requirement. C: physical access control concerns entry to facilities.
notes.explanation: The control requires approved changes only, with changes and their impacts documented.
notes.evidence: Implement only organization-approved changes to the system, component, or service;
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-10 Developer Configuration Management, PDF p. 300

notes.front: A bank’s board approves a security test that its technology staff are not told about, to see how much damage a real attacker could do. Which kind of testing is this?
notes.back: Covert (black hat) testing.
notes.choices:
A) Overt (white hat) testing
B) Covert (black hat) testing
C) A tabletop exercise
notes.choicesExplained: A: overt testing is done with the staff’s knowledge and consent. C: a tabletop exercise is a discussion of a contingency plan, not a live test.
notes.explanation: Testing without the staff’s knowledge but with upper management’s permission, to examine an adversary’s possible impact, is covert testing.
notes.evidence: Covert security testing, also known as black hat testing, takes an adversarial approach by performing testing without the knowledge of the organization’s IT staff but with the full knowledge and permission of upper management.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment, Section 2.4.2 Overt and Covert, PDF p. 16

notes.front: A team keeps the definition of its build and deployment pipeline in a version-controlled file, instead of setting it up by hand in a console. Which toolchain practice from the Secure Software Development Framework is this?
notes.back: Code-based configuration for toolchains (pipelines-as-code).
notes.choices:
A) Code-based configuration for toolchains
B) Archiving each software release
C) Root cause analysis
notes.choicesExplained: B: archiving preserves releases to study vulnerabilities later. C: root cause analysis studies vulnerabilities once found.
notes.explanation: The framework gives pipelines-as-code as an example of following recommended practices for tools and toolchains.
notes.evidence: Example 3: Use code-based configuration for toolchains (e.g., pipelines-as-code, toolchains-as-code).
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PO.3, Implement Supporting Toolchains, PDF p. 16

notes.front: While modelling threats to a new cloud service, a team decides not to mitigate one risk and gets an exception approved. What should it record, according to the Secure Software Development Framework?
notes.back: The response to the risk and the rationale for the approved exception.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, as the risk is not being mitigated
B) The response and the rationale for the exception
C) Only the name of the approver
notes.choicesExplained: A: the framework asks for a record of every risk’s response, including exceptions. C: the rationale, not just who approved it, is what the framework asks to be recorded.
notes.explanation: The framework asks teams to record each risk’s response, how mitigations will be achieved and why exceptions were approved.
notes.evidence: Record the response to each risk, including how mitigations are to be achieved and what the rationales are for any approved exceptions to the security requirements.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1, Practice PW.1, Design Software to Meet Security Requirements and Mitigate Security Risks, PDF p. 20

notes.front: A payment app catches errors only at the top level, so when a network call fails mid-transaction it carries on in an unknown state and posts duplicate payments. Which Top 10:2025 category is this?
notes.back: Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.
notes.choices:
A) Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
B) Injection
C) Security Logging and Alerting Failures
notes.choicesExplained: B: no untrusted input is run as a command. C: the failure is in handling the error, not in logging or alerting on it.
notes.explanation: Late, high-level error handling that leaves the system in an unpredictable state is among the causes the page lists for this category.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10:2025, A10:2025 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions, Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A product security lead wants evidence on which classes of software weakness are most common and most impactful, to decide what developers should be trained on first. Which list fits best?
notes.back: The CWE Top 25.
notes.choices:
A) The CWE Top 25
B) The STRIDE model
C) The recovery time objective
notes.choicesExplained: B: STRIDE sorts threats to a design into categories; it does not rank real-world weaknesses. C: a recovery time objective sets how long a resource may be unavailable.
notes.explanation: Its publishers say it gives insight into common root causes and exploitability, which supports risk prioritisation.
notes.evidence: Exploitability Insights – Certain weaknesses such as command injection attract adversarial attention, enabling risk prioritization.
notes.source: MITRE, 2025 CWE Top 25 Most Dangerous Software Weaknesses, 2025 Top 25 List
notes.sourceLicence: B · CWE terms of use (MITRE royalty-free licence)

notes.front: How does static code analysis differ from dynamic code analysis?
notes.back: Static analysis checks code, and included libraries, without running it; dynamic analysis verifies the program at runtime.
notes.explanation: Special Publication 800-53 describes dynamic analysis as runtime verification using tools that monitor running programs.
notes.evidence: Dynamic code analysis provides runtime verification of software programs using tools capable of monitoring programs
notes.source: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations, SA-11(8) Developer Testing and Evaluation — Dynamic Code Analysis, PDF p. 306

notes.front: How does overt (white hat) security testing differ from covert (black hat) testing?
notes.back: Overt testing has the staff’s knowledge and consent; covert testing is hidden from staff but approved by upper management.
notes.explanation: Overt testing allows a comprehensive evaluation; covert testing examines what damage an adversary could cause.
notes.evidence: Overt security testing, also known as white hat testing, involves performing external and/or internal testing with the knowledge and consent of the organization’s IT staff, enabling comprehensive evaluation of the network or system security posture.
notes.source: NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment, Section 2.4.2 Overt and Covert, PDF p. 16

notes.front: How does broken object level authorisation differ from broken function level authorisation?
notes.back: Object level: no check on access to the object an identifier names. Function level: users reach functions, such as administrative ones, beyond their role.
notes.explanation: Both are authorisation flaws in the 2023 interface security list, ranked first and fifth.
notes.source: OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks – 2023, OWASP Top 10 API Security Risks – 2023, Risk Description
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does spoofing differ from elevation of privilege in STRIDE?
notes.back: Spoofing uses another user’s authentication information; elevation of privilege is an unprivileged user gaining privileged access.
notes.explanation: One borrows someone else’s identity; the other raises one’s own level of access.
notes.source: Microsoft Learn, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool threats, STRIDE model
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
